did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the Lord answering Job, continuing directly from the Lord’s appearance to him out of the storm.
Job says, “Behold, I am insignificant,” acknowledging his limited position; he declares that he has put his hand over his mouth, meaning that he has chosen to remain silent.
The Lord poses a fundamental question to Job: Will he annul God’s judgment and condemn the Lord in order to justify himself?
The Lord says that if Job can save himself by his own strength, then the Lord will also acknowledge him; this challenge highlights the limits of human power.
Behemoth is described as a creature made by the Lord that feeds on grass like cattle; the text does not explicitly identify it with any particular animal known today.
Behemoth’s bones are described as “channels of bronze” and as being like bars of iron, expressing its extraordinary strength.
Despite its size and strength, Behemoth is described as lying under the shade among the reeds and marsh plants; it is part of nature and is not presented merely as a destructive creature.
Behemoth is not frightened by a raging river; even when the Jordan surges up to its mouth, it is portrayed as confident and unhurried.
The passage about Leviathan begins by asking whether a person can pull it out with a hook or tie down its tongue with a rope; these questions emphasize that it cannot easily be controlled.
The Lord asks whether anyone can make a bargain with Leviathan, take it as a lifelong servant, or play with it like a bird; this highlights the creature’s independence and power.
